questions.q: What does this lesson mean by saying "being right isn't enough"?
options: An architecturally correct decision that nobody with budget authority agrees to never actually gets implemented, so in practical terms it delivered nothing
Technical architects are never actually correct about tradeoffs
Executive stakeholders are always right and architects are always wrong
Correctness only matters for centralized governance decisions
questions.explain: A decision's real value includes whether it survives contact with the people who have to fund and approve it — correctness alone doesn't implement anything.

questions.q: Why don't executive stakeholders share an architect's technical vocabulary, according to this lesson?
options: They're evaluating a different question than the architect is, in terms of cost, risk, and timeline rather than technical tradeoffs
They are less capable of understanding architecture decisions
They have no real stake in the platform's outcome
They were never given a chance to attend the same training courses
questions.explain: The gap isn't ability — it's that executives evaluate decisions through cost, risk, and timeline, which is a legitimate but different lens than the technical framing.

questions.q: When translating a technical tradeoff for an executive audience, what should stay the same?
options: The underlying decision, cost, and risk — only the vocabulary used to describe it changes
Nothing; translation means simplifying away the real tradeoff
The technical terminology, left exactly as-is
The recommendation, which should always favor the cheaper option regardless of risk
questions.explain: Honest translation recasts the same real tradeoff in terms an executive can evaluate — it doesn't quietly change what the tradeoff actually is.

questions.q: When Finance wants tight approval controls and Marketing wants minimal-friction self-service on the same platform investment, what is the architect's real job?
options: Surface the actual tradeoff explicitly and let stakeholders with budget authority make an informed decision
Decide privately which department's priority is correct and build to that silently
Refuse to build anything until both departments agree on every detail
Default to whichever department asked first
questions.explain: Treating one department's priority as simply correct and routing around the other erodes trust; naming the real tradeoff and letting budget authority decide is the honest path.

questions.q: How does this lesson define real "buy-in," as opposed to simple approval?
options: Stakeholders who genuinely understand a decision and will defend it later, not just a signature obtained once
A verbal agreement given in a hallway conversation
Any approval, regardless of whether the stakeholder understood the tradeoff
Buy-in from the platform team only, with no need for executive involvement
questions.explain: Genuine buy-in means the stakeholder understands the tradeoff well enough to defend it when it's questioned again later, which is a higher bar than a one-time sign-off.
